claim: The synaptonemal complex (SC) is a tripartite proteinaceous structure comprised of lateral element proteins running along the axes of the homologs and central region proteins connecting these axes.
source: The SC is a ladder-like structure comprised of lateral element proteins running along the axes of the homologs and central region proteins connecting these axes (Colaiácovo, 2006; Page and Hawley, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Colaiácovo, 2006; Page and Hawley, 2003) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The SC is required to stabilize the interactions between pairs of homologous chromosomes and for interhomolog crossover (CO) formation in budding yeast, worms, flies, and mice.
source: The SC is required to stabilize the interactions between pairs of homologous chromosomes and for interhomolog crossover (CO) formation in budding yeast, worms, flies, and mice (Nag et al., 1995; Storlazzi et al., 1996; Page and Hawley, 2001; MacQueen et al., 2002; Colaiácovo et al., 2003; de Vries et al., 2005; Smolikov et al., 2007a; 2007b; 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work across different model organisms.

claim: The SC must be disassembled prior to the end of prophase I to ensure timely and proper chromosome segregation.
source: Importantly, the SC must be disassembled prior to the end of prophase I to ensure timely and proper chromosome segregation (Sourirajan and Lichten, 2008; Jordan et al., 2009; Dix et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several proteins have been implicated in regulating the disassembly of SC proteins, including polo-like kinase in mammals and budding yeast, Ipl1/Aurora B kinase in budding yeast, the condensin complex component dcap-g in flies and both AKIR-1 and ZHP-3 in worms.
source: Several proteins have been recently implicated in regulating the disassembly of SC proteins, including polo-like kinase in mammals and budding yeast, Ipl1/Aurora B kinase in budding yeast, the condensin complex component dcap-g in flies and both AKIR-1 (a member of the akirin protein family) and ZHP-3 (ortholog of budding yeast Zip3) in worms (Sourirajan and Lichten, 2008; Jordan et al., 2009; Resnick et al., 2009; Jordan et al., 2012; Clemons et al., 2013; Bhalla et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SC disassembles asymmetrically in C. elegans, progressing from being localized along the full length of the interface between homologous chromosomes in early prophase to persisting at discrete chromosome locations termed the short arm domains at late prophase I.
source: We previously showed that the SC disassembles asymmetrically in C. elegans, progressing from being localized along the full length of the interface between homologous chromosomes in early prophase to persisting at discrete chromosome locations, termed the short arm domains, corresponding to one end of every pair of homologs at late prophase I (Figure 1A) (Nabeshima et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Nabeshima et al., 2005) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In C. elegans, a single CO occurs at the terminal third of every pair of homologous chromosomes.
source: Since in C. elegans, a single CO occurs at the terminal third of every pair of homologous chromosomes, we proposed that chromosomes remodel around the single off-centered CO event at the pachytene-diplotene transition.
evidence: This claim is stated as an established fact in the field.

claim: Chromosomes remodel around the single off-centered CO event at the pachytene-diplotene transition, resulting in bivalents with a cruciform configuration comprised of two perpendicular chromosomal axes (the long and short arm domains) intersecting at the chiasma.
source: we proposed that chromosomes remodel around the single off-centered CO event at the pachytene-diplotene transition. This results in bivalents with a cruciform configuration comprised of two perpendicular chromosomal axes (namely the long and short arm domains) intersecting at the chiasma, where the long arms face the poles and the short arms occupy an equatorial position on the metaphase plate (Figure 1A) (Nabeshima et al., 2005; Riddle et al., 1997; Maddox et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Asymmetric disassembly of the SC has been observed in yeast, flies and mice, with residual localized retention of the SC at centromeres.
source: Subsequent studies in yeast, flies and mice (Newnham et al., 2010; Qiao et al., 2012; Bisig et al., 2012; Takeo et al., 2011; Gladstone et al., 2009) also observed an asymmetric disassembly of the SC, with a residual localized retention of the SC at centromeres.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ect-2 was identified in a targeted RNAi screen for novel components regulating chromosome remodeling and short/long arm identity by using the mislocalization of Aurora B kinase, AIR-2, as a readout.
source: We identified ect-2, the homolog of mammalian Rho GEF, in a targeted RNAi screen for novel components regulating chromosome remodeling and short/long arm identity by using the mislocalization of Aurora B kinase, AIR-2, which localizes to the short arms of diakinesis bivalents in wild type oocytes as a readout (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach used to identify ect-2.

claim: ECT-2 is a highly conserved protein initially identified as a proto-oncogene in cell culture.
source: ECT-2 (Epithelial Cell Transforming sequence 2) is a highly conserved protein, initially identified as a proto-oncogene in cell culture (Miki et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Miki et al., 1993).

claim: ECT-2 encodes a Guanine nucleotide Exchange Factor (GEF) that belongs to the Dbl family and functions as a key activator of Rho GTPase mediated signaling.
source: It encodes a Guanine nucleotide Exchange Factor (GEF) that belongs to the Dbl family and functions as a key activator of Rho GTPase mediated signaling with roles during cytokinesis, DNA damage-induced cell death, cell polarity establishment during embryogenesis, vulval development, and epidermal P cell migration (Prokopenko et al., 1999; Saito et al., 2003; Morita et al., 2005; Srougi and Burridge, 2011; Canevascini et al., 2005; Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ECT2 is expressed in testis and ovaries in humans.
source: Although ECT2 is expressed in testis and ovaries in humans (Hirata et al., 2009; Fields and Justilien, 2010), understanding its role during mammalian meiosis is challenging due to its earlier roles in development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hirata et al., 2009; Fields and Justilien, 2010).

claim: ect-2(ax751rf) reduction-of-function mutants exhibit a failure of AIR-2 to load on the chromosomes in late diakinesis.
source: Analysis of ect-2(ax751rf) temperature-sensitive reduction-of-function mutants and of worms depleted of ect-2 by RNAi revealed a failure of AIR-2 to load on the chromosomes in late diakinesis even though AIR-2 is present inside the nucleus (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ect-2(ax751rf) mutants exhibit a reduced brood size, increased embryonic lethality and a High Incidence of Males (Him) at the non-permissive temperature.
source: ect-2(ax751rf) mutants also exhibited a reduced brood size, increased embryonic lethality and a High Incidence of Males (Him) at the non-permissive temperature, all phenotypes indicative of increased meiotic chromosome nondisjunction (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: ect-2(e1778) null mutants are sterile and exhibit fewer germ cells with abnormal nuclei.
source: Importantly, we shifted ect-2(ax751rf) worms to the non-permissive temperature at the L4 larval stage to bypass the requirements for ECT-2 during somatic development and germ cell mitotic proliferation such as seen in ect-2(e1778) null mutants, which are sterile and exhibit fewer germ cells with abnormal nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ECT-2::GFP is able to rescue the reduced brood size, embryonic lethality and Him phenotypes observed in the ect-2(ax751rf) mutants.
source: ECT-2::GFP is able to rescue the reduced brood size, embryonic lethality and Him phenotypes observed in the ect-2(ax751rf) mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), confirming that mutation of ect-2 impairs fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: ECT-2::GFP localizes throughout the germline from the mitotically dividing nuclei at the premeiotic tip to the end of diakinesis.
source: We found that ECT-2::GFP localizes throughout the germline from the mitotically dividing nuclei at the premeiotic tip, where it is enriched at the germ cell membrane, to the end of diakinesis, where it exhibits a stronger nuclear signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: In ect-2(ax751rf) mutants, SC formation is indistinguishable from wild type in most of the meiotic nuclei except for a few pachytene nuclei (11.1%) which display reduced SC assembly.
source: In ect-2(ax751rf) mutants, SC formation is indistinguishable from wild type in most of the meiotic nuclei except for a few pachytene nuclei (11.1%, n=120/1080 pachytene nuclei) which display reduced SC assembly (Figures 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: In ect-2(ax751rf) mutants, SC disassembly occurred as in wild type, initiating in late pachytene and resulting in the restricted localization of the central region proteins of the SC to the short arm of the bivalents.
source: SC disassembly occurred as in wild type, initiating in late pachytene and resulting in the restricted localization of the central region proteins of the SC, as exemplified by SYP-1, to the short arm of the bivalents (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ect-2(zh8gf) gain-of-function mutants exhibited defects in both SC assembly and disassembly at the non-permissive temperature.
source: In contrast, ect-2(zh8gf) gain-of-function mutants, in which a mutation in an auto-inhibitory BRCT domain retains ECT-2 in its constitutively active configuration (Canevascini et al., 2005), exhibited defects in both SC assembly and disassembly at the non-permissive temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by data and a citation to prior work (Canevascini et al., 2005).

claim: In ect-2(zh8gf) mutants, the SC failed to assemble on the chromosomes and instead SYP-1 formed aggregates referred to as polycomplexes.
source: Specifically, the SC failed to assemble on the chromosomes and instead SYP-1 formed aggregates referred to as polycomplexes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In ect-2(zh8gf) mutants, nuclei that had already gone through the leptotene/zygotene stage before the temperature shift showed normal synapsis during early and mid pachytene stages, but the central region components of the SC remained localized along the long arms of the bivalents and failed to become restricted to the short arms during late prophase.
source: Those nuclei that had already gone through the leptotene/zygotene stage before the temperature shift showed normal synapsis during early and mid pachytene stages, but the central region components of the SC remained localized along the long arms of the bivalents and failed to become restricted to the short arms during late prophase (a defect herein referred to as impaired disassembly of the SC proteins) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The HORMA domain containing lateral element protein HTP-3 exhibits a wild type pattern of localization in ect-2 mutants.
source: Importantly, the HORMA domain containing lateral element protein HTP-3, exhibits a wild type pattern of localization in ect-2 mutants (Figures 1C,D and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1C, D and 2.

claim: ECT-2 acts in a specific manner to regulate SC dynamics, which involves regulating central region components of the SC.
source: This suggests that ECT-2 acts in a specific manner to regulate SC dynamics, which involves regulating central region components of the SC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that HTP-3 localization is normal while central region components are affected.

claim: AIR-2 localization is still successfully restricted to the short arms of the bivalents at diakinesis in ect-2(zh8gf) mutants.
source: First, we observed that AIR-2 localization is still successfully restricted to the short arms of the bivalents at diakinesis in ect-2(zh8gf) mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LAB-1 is still lost from the short arms and restricted to the long arms of the bivalents in ect-2(zh8gf) mutants as in wild type.
source: Second, LAB-1, a proposed functional ortholog of Shugoshin, is still lost from the short arms and restricted to the long arms of the bivalents as in wild type (de Carvalho et al., 2008; Schvarzstein et al., 2010; Tzur et al., 2012) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior work.

claim: Key aspects of late prophase chromosome remodeling, namely LAB-1 and AIR-2 restricted localizations, are not altered in ect-2(zh8gf) mutants.
source: These data indicate that key aspects of late prophase chromosome remodeling, namely LAB-1 and AIR-2 restricted localizations, are not altered in ect-2(zh8gf) mutants and that ECT-2 specifically regulates the disassembly of the SC proteins during prophase I of meiosis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing normal AIR-2 and LAB-1 localization.

claim: ECT-2 has been shown to activate the RAS/MAP kinase signaling cascade to promote primary vulval cell fate specification during vulval development in C. elegans.
source: ECT-2 has been shown to activate the RAS/MAP kinase signaling cascade to promote primary vulval cell fate specification during vulval development in C. elegans (Canevascini et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Canevascini et al., 2005).

claim: The ERK MAP kinase, MPK-1, is expressed in both somatic tissues as well as in the germline where it controls several aspects of germ line development including pachytene progression and germ cell survival.
source: In C. elegans, the ERK MAP kinase, MPK-1, is expressed in both somatic tissues as well as in the germline where it controls several aspects of germ line development including pachytene progression and germ cell survival (Church et al., 1995; Kritikou et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: mpk-1(ga117) null, mpk-1(ga111lf) and mpk-1(ku1lf) temperature-sensitive loss-of-function mutants revealed defects in SC assembly as indicated by the formation of polycomplexes at the non-permissive temperature.
source: Analysis of mpk-1(ga117) null, mpk-1(ga111lf) and mpk-1(ku1lf) temperature-sensitive loss-of-function mutants revealed defects in SC assembly as indicated by the formation of polycomplexes, similar to ect-2(zh8gf) mutants at the non-permissive temperature (Figure 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Germline nuclei that had already passed through the leptotene/zygotene stage before the temperature shift exhibited normal SC tracts along chromosomes at the pachytene stage in mpk-1 mutants.
source: However, germline nuclei that had already passed through the leptotene/zygotene stage before the temperature shift exhibited normal SC tracts along chromosomes at the pachytene stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Nuclei fail to progress from early/mid-pachytene to late-pachytene in mpk-1(ga117) null mutants.
source: Since nuclei fail to progress from early/mid-pachytene to late-pachytene in mpk-1(ga117) null mutants (Lee et al., 2007), we analyzed the disassembly of SC proteins in mpk-1(ga111lf) mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Lee et al., 2007).

claim: Nuclei that were able to progress from pachytene to diplotene exhibited normal SC disassembly in mpk-1(ga111lf) mutants similar to the ect-2(ax751rf) mutant.
source: Nuclei that were able to progress from pachytene to diplotene exhibited normal SC disassembly similar to the ect-2(ax751rf) mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: let-60(ga89gf) temperature-sensitive gain-of-function mutant leads to constitutive activation of MAP kinase both in somatic tissues and the germline.
source: A let-60(ga89gf) temperature-sensitive gain-of-function mutant leads to constitutive activation of MAP kinase both in somatic tissues and the germline (Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Lee et al., 2007).

claim: let-60(ga89gf) mutants exhibit defects in both SC assembly, as evidenced by the presence of polycomplexes, and the disassembly of the SC proteins from the long arms of the bivalents at the non-permissive temperature.
source: Similar to the ect-2(zh8gf) mutant, let-60(ga89gf) mutants exhibit defects in both SC assembly, as evidenced by the presence of polycomplexes, and the disassembly of the SC proteins from the long arms of the bivalents, where they persisted at the non-permissive temperature (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: lip-1(zh15rf) reduction-of-function mutants exhibit defects in the disassembly of SC proteins.
source: Similar defects in the disassembly of SC proteins are also observed in the lip-1(zh15rf) reduction-of-function mutant (Figure 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In lip-1(zh15rf) mutants, the LIP-1 phosphatase fails to inactivate MPK-1 in late pachytene, which therefore persists throughout pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis.
source: where the LIP-1 phosphatase fails to inactivate, MPK-1 in late pachytene, which therefore persists throughout pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis (Hajnal and Berset, 2002; Rutkowski et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hajnal and Berset, 2002; Rutkowski et al., 2011).

claim: The constitutive presence of active MPK-1 impairs the disassembly of SC proteins from the long arms of the bivalents.
source: suggesting that the constitutive presence of active MPK-1 impairs the disassembly of SC proteins from the long arms of the bivalents.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mutants with persistent MPK-1 activity show SC disassembly defects.

claim: No defects in SC assembly were observed in lip-1(zh15rf) mutants.
source: In contrast, we did not observe any defects in SC assembly in lip-1(zh15rf) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: LAB-1 localization was not altered in either let-60(ga89gf) or lip-1(zh15rf) mutants.
source: Further, we found that LAB-1 localization was not altered in either let-60(ga89gf) or lip-1(zh15rf) mutants suggesting that MAP kinase specifically regulates the disassembly of SC proteins from the long arms of the bivalents and not other aspects of late prophase chromosome remodeling (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: MAP kinase specifically regulates the disassembly of SC proteins from the long arms of the bivalents and not other aspects of late prophase chromosome remodeling.
source: suggesting that MAP kinase specifically regulates the disassembly of SC proteins from the long arms of the bivalents and not other aspects of late prophase chromosome remodeling (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that LAB-1 localization is normal while SC disassembly is affected.

claim: In the ect-2(ax751rf) mutant, there is reduced dpMPK-1 signal in the mid-late pachytene region compared to wild type.
source: In the ect-2(ax751rf) mutant, we see reduced dpMPK-1 signal in the mid-late pachytene region compared to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: Partial depletion of rho-1 results in reduced dpMPK-1 signal in the mid-late pachytene region.
source: Similarly to the ect-2(ax751rf) mutant, partial depletion of rho-1 also results in reduced dpMPK-1 signal in the mid-late pachytene region (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The expression pattern of RHO-1 is similar to that observed for ECT-2 in the germline.
source: In addition, the expression pattern of RHO-1 is similar to that observed for ECT-2 in the germline (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: dpMPK-1 expression is not turned off at late pachytene and during diplotene in the ect-2(zh8gf) mutant.
source: In contrast to ect-2(ax751rf) mutants and to rho-1 partial knock down, dpMPK-1 expression is not turned off at late pachytene and during diplotene in the ect-2(zh8gf) mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: dpMPK-1 persists from pachytene to diakinesis in ect-2(zh8gf) mutants similar to let-60/RAS gain-of-function mutants.
source: Instead, dpMPK-1 persists from pachytene to diakinesis similar to let-60/RAS gain-of-function mutants (Figure 2—figure supplements 5A and B; [Lee et al., 2007]).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B and a citation to prior work (Lee et al., 2007).

claim: ECT-2 and RHO-1 either promote MPK-1 activation or block MPK-1 inactivation in the germline.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that ECT-2 and RHO-1 either promote MPK-1 activation or block MPK-1 inactivation in the germline.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that loss of ECT-2 or RHO-1 reduces dpMPK-1 signal while gain-of-function ECT-2 increases it.

claim: let-60(ga89gf) mutants exhibit a severely reduced brood size compared to ect-2(ax751rf).
source: let-60(ga89gf) mutants exhibit a severely reduced brood size compared to ect-2(ax751rf).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: ect-2(ax751rf); let-60(ga89gf) double mutants exhibit a severely reduced brood size similar to let-60(ga89gf).
source: Interestingly, ect-2(ax751rf); let-60(ga89gf) double mutants exhibit a severely reduced brood size similar to let-60(ga89gf).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: ect-2(ax751rf); let-60(ga89gf) double mutants exhibit defects in the disassembly of SC proteins similar to let-60(ga89gf) mutants.
source: Further, ect-2(ax751rf); let-60(ga89gf) double mutants exhibit defects in the disassembly of SC proteins similar to let-60(ga89gf) mutants (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: LET-60 functions downstream of ECT-2 in the germline.
source: These data show that LET-60 functions downstream of ECT-2 in the germline.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the epistasis analysis showing that let-60(gf) phenotype is epistatic to ect-2(rf).

claim: mpk-1(ga111lf) is able to suppress the SC disassembly defect of ect-2(zh8gf) mutants.
source: We found that mpk-1(ga111lf) is able to suppress the SC disassembly defect of ect-2(zh8gf) mutants (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ECT-2 functions through the MAP Kinase pathway to regulate the disassembly of the SC proteins on the long arms of the bivalents.
source: Thus, our data demonstrates that ECT-2 functions through the MAP Kinase pathway to regulate the disassembly of the SC proteins on the long arms of the bivalents uncovering a novel mode of regulation for this structure.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the epistasis analysis and dpMPK-1 localization data.

claim: SYP-1, SYP-2, and SYP-4 contain potential MAP kinase phosphorylation sites as predicted by phosphorylation site predictor programs GPS 2.1 and KinasePhos 2.0.
source: This identified potential MAP kinase phosphorylation sites on SYP-1, SYP-2, SYP-4 and none on SYP-3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SYP-2 is phosphorylated at S25, a potential MAP kinase phosphorylation site, as confirmed by mass spectrometry analysis.
source: These combined approaches confirmed that SYP-2 is phosphorylated at S25, a potential MAP kinase phosphorylation site (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The germline-specific isoform of MPK-1 co-immunoprecipitates with SYP-2 confirming the in vivo interaction.
source: We next determined that SYP-2 interacts with the germline-specific isoform of MPK-1 in vivo by immunoprecipitating SYP-2 from the lysates of adult worms expressing endogenous SYP-2 as well as SYP-2::GFP and probing with an MPK-1 antibody on western blots (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SYP-2 protein co-immunoprecipitates with dpMPK-1 in pull downs from adult worm lysates.
source: The reciprocal experiment showed that the SYP-2 protein co-immunoprecipitates with dpMPK-1 in pull downs from adult worm lysates (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SYP-2 is phosphorylated in vivo and exists in both phosphorylated as well as unphosphorylated forms.
source: This shows that SYP-2 is phosphorylated in vivo and that SYP-2 exists in both phosphorylated as well as unphosphorylated forms.
evidence: This claim is supported by CIP assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In mpk-1(ga117) null mutants, the upper band corresponding to phosphorylated SYP-2 is not present, suggesting that phosphorylation of SYP-2 is dependent on MAP kinase.
source: Further, in mpk-1(ga117) null mutants, the upper band corresponding to phosphorylated SYP-2 is not present, suggesting that phosphorylation of SYP-2 is dependent on MAP kinase.
evidence: This claim is supported by CIP assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In let-60(ga89gf)/RAS gain-of-function mutants, two bands corresponding to the phosphorylated and unphosphorylated SYP-2 protein are detected.
source: In let-60(ga89gf)/RAS gain-of-function mutants, we detect two bands corresponding to the phosphorylated and unphosphorylated SYP-2 protein, instead of only the phosphorylated band.
evidence: This claim is supported by CIP assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Only a subset of the SYP-2 protein is phosphorylated by MPK-1.
source: This could be due to only a subset of the SYP-2 protein being phosphorylated by MPK-1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both phosphorylated and unphosphorylated forms are detected in gain-of-function mutants.

claim: SYP-2 could be phosphorylated by dpMPK-1 at the mid to late-pachytene region thereby regulating the localization of SYP-2 in a spatio-temporal manner.
source: This is consistent with the expression pattern of MPK-1 in the germline where the active form of dpMPK-1 is expressed only from mid to late pachytene. Meanwhile, SYP-2 is expressed from the leptotene/zygotene stage to late diakinesis. Therefore, SYP-2 could be phosphorylated by dpMPK-1 at the mid to late-pachytene region thereby regulating the localization of SYP-2 in a spatio-temporal manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression patterns of dpMPK-1 and SYP-2.

claim: The SYP-2 (S25A) phosphodead mutant protein runs at the same size of the unphosphorylated SYP-2 band, suggesting that there are no additional phosphorylation sites in the SYP-2 protein.
source: Further, we found that the SYP-2 (S25A) phosphodead mutant protein runs at the same size of the unphosphorylated SYP-2 band, suggesting that there are no additional phosphorylation sites in the SYP-2 protein (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CIP assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SYP-2 was phosphorylated by MAP kinase at the S25 site in vitro in the presence of ERK MAP kinase.
source: We found that SYP-2 was phosphorylated by MAP kinase at the S25 site in vitro in the presence of ERK MAP kinase (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The phosphorylated peptide was not observed in the absence of the kinase or when the kinase reaction was subsequently incubated with lambda phosphatase.
source: The phosphorylated peptide was not observed in the absence of the kinase or when the kinase reaction was subsequently incubated with lambda phosphatase.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data.

claim: In vivo phosphorylation of SYP-2 is dependent on the MAP kinase pathway.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that in vivo phosphorylation of SYP-2 is dependent on the MAP kinase pathway and that SYP-2 is an in vitro phosphorylation substrate of the ERK MAP kinase.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CIP assay and in vitro kinase assay data.

claim: SYP-2 is an in vitro phosphorylation substrate of the ERK MAP kinase.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that in vivo phosphorylation of SYP-2 is dependent on the MAP kinase pathway and that SYP-2 is an in vitro phosphorylation substrate of the ERK MAP kinase.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: No defects in either SC assembly or disassembly were observed in the syp-2 phosphodead mutant.
source: We did not observe defects in either SC assembly or disassembly in the syp-2 phosphodead mutant (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the syp-2 phosphomimetic mutant, SC assembly was normal, but the disassembly of SC proteins was impaired as exemplified by SYP-1, SYP-2, SYP-3 and SYP-4 persisting on the long arms and failing to become restricted to the short arms of the bivalents.
source: However, in the syp-2 phosphomimetic mutant, while SC assembly was normal, the disassembly of SC proteins was impaired as exemplified by SYP-1, SYP-2, SYP-3 and SYP-4 persisting on the long arms and failing to become restricted to the short arms of the bivalents (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: All four SYP proteins are interdependent on each other for their localization.
source: This is consistent with the observation that constitutive activation of dpMPK-1 leads to failure in disassembly of SC proteins from the long arm of the bivalents (this study), and that all four SYP proteins are interdependent on each other for their localization (Colaiácovo et al., 2003; Smolikov et al., 2007a; 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Colaiácovo et al., 2003; Smolikov et al., 2007a; 2009).

claim: Other aspects of late prophase chromosome remodeling, such as AIR-2 and LAB-1 restricted localizations, are not altered in either the syp-2 phosphodead or phosphomimetic mutants.
source: Other aspects of late prophase chromosome remodeling, such as AIR-2 and LAB-1 restricted localizations, are not altered in either the syp-2 phosphodead or phosphomimetic mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and 4.

claim: syp-2 phosphomimetic mutants exhibit a reduction in brood size (109 ± 32), accompanied by 14.3% embryonic lethality and 2.1% males.
source: However, we see a reduction in brood size (109 ± 32), accompanied by 14.3% embryonic lethality and 2.1% males, in syp-2 phosphomimetic mutants indicating that impaired disassembly of the SC proteins results in defects in chromosome segregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by brood size and phenotypic analysis data.

claim: Impaired disassembly of the SC proteins results in defects in chromosome segregation.
source: indicating that impaired disassembly of the SC proteins results in defects in chromosome segregation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that syp-2 phosphomimetic mutants show both SC disassembly defects and chromosome segregation defects.

claim: Phosphorylation of SYP-2 protein at the S25 site prevents the disassembly of the SC proteins from the long arm of the bivalents during late prophase.
source: Taken together, our data show that phosphorylation of SYP-2 protein at the S25 site prevents the disassembly of the SC proteins from the long arm of the bivalents during late prophase.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the phosphomimetic mutant shows impaired SC disassembly.

claim: A two-step CO specification process has been described to take place following SC assembly as prospective CO sites progressively differentiate during C. elegans and mouse meiosis.
source: Recently, a two-step CO specification process has been described to take place following SC assembly as prospective CO sites progressively differentiate during C. elegans and mouse meiosis (Yokoo et al., 2012; Holloway et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Yokoo et al., 2012; Holloway et al., 2014).

claim: CO specification consists of CO licensing during mid-pachytene followed by CO designation at or just prior to the mid-to-late pachytene transition in a manner dependent of the pro-CO factor COSA-1/CNTD1.
source: This consists of CO licensing during mid-pachytene followed by CO designation at or just prior to the mid-to-late pachytene transition in a manner dependent of the pro-CO factor COSA-1/CNTD1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Active dpMPK-1 and foci for the pro-CO factor COSA-1 are both observed at the same time in pachytene stage nuclei.
source: First, active dpMPK-1 and foci for the pro-CO factor COSA-1 are both observed at the same time in pachytene stage nuclei suggesting a correlation between CO precursors and active MPK-1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a significant persistence of dpMPK-1 signal in zhp-3 and cosa-1 mutants compared to wild type.
source: Second, we observed a significant persistence of dpMPK-1 signal in zhp-3 and cosa-1 mutants compared to wild type suggesting that inactivation of MPK-1 is linked to formation of a CO precursor (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Inactivation of MPK-1 is linked to formation of a CO precursor.
source: suggesting that inactivation of MPK-1 is linked to formation of a CO precursor (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that dpMPK-1 persists in CO-defective mutants.

claim: The defect in disassembly of SC proteins observed in cosa-1 mutants is fully rescued in a cosa-1 mpk-1(lf) double mutant.
source: Third, the defect in disassembly of SC proteins observed in cosa-1 mutants is fully rescued in a cosa-1 mpk-1(lf) double mutant and partly rescued in ect-2(rf);cosa-1 and cosa-1;syp-2(S25A) double mutants (11.5% and 40.9% suppression of the cosa-1 disassembly defect phenotype, respectively) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The defect in disassembly of SC proteins observed in cosa-1 mutants is partly rescued in ect-2(rf);cosa-1 and cosa-1;syp-2(S25A) double mutants (11.5% and 40.9% suppression of the cosa-1 disassembly defect phenotype, respectively).
source: Third, the defect in disassembly of SC proteins observed in cosa-1 mutants is fully rescued in a cosa-1 mpk-1(lf) double mutant and partly rescued in ect-2(rf);cosa-1 and cosa-1;syp-2(S25A) double mutants (11.5% and 40.9% suppression of the cosa-1 disassembly defect phenotype, respectively) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There may be additional kinases regulating the other SYP proteins in an MPK-1-dependent manner.
source: The cosa-1; syp-2(S25A) partial rescue leads us to hypothesize that there may be additional kinases regulating the other SYP proteins in an MPK-1-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the partial rescue observed.

claim: There are additional phosphorylation sites for other kinases, such as the polo-like kinase, on SYP-1 and SYP-4, verified by mass spectrometry.
source: Indeed, while we did not find evidence for additional MPK-1 phosphorylation sites on SYP-2, there are additional phosphorylation sites for other kinases, such as the polo-like kinase, on SYP-1 and SYP-4, verified by mass spectrometry (Nadarajan and Colaiacovo, unpublished and PHOSIDA (http://www.phosida.com)
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data and database information.

claim: Polo-like kinase itself was identified as a target of MPK-1 in C. elegans.
source: and Polo-like kinase itself was identified as a target of MPK-1 in C. elegans (Arur et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Arur et al., 2009).

claim: MPK-1 plays a role in coordinating recognition of a CO precursor with asymmetric disassembly of SC proteins.
source: While the roles exerted by these additional kinases on the SC remain to be investigated, our observations support a role for MPK-1 in coordinating recognition of a CO precursor with asymmetric disassembly of SC proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic and localization data.

claim: MPK-1 is inactivated in response to CO designation resulting in either de novo loading of unphosphorylated SYP-2 or dephosphorylation of chromatin-associated SYP-2, which triggers disassembly of SC proteins from along the long arms.
source: Therefore, we propose a model in which MPK-1 is inactivated in response to CO designation resulting in either de novo loading of unphosphorylated SYP-2 or dephosphorylation of chromatin-associated SYP-2, which triggers disassembly of SC proteins from along the long arms.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented.

claim: Coordination between CO designation and the disassembly of SC proteins executed via a conserved MAP kinase pathway is critical for ensuring accurate chromosome segregation during meiosis.
source: Thus, coordination between CO designation and the disassembly of SC proteins executed via a conserved MAP kinase pathway is critical for ensuring accurate chromosome segregation during meiosis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that defects in this coordination lead to chromosome segregation errors.

claim: The SC disassembles asymmetrically and persists associated with the centromere until late prophase in both yeast and flies.
source: This process occurs not only in C. elegans, but also in budding yeast, flies and mice. In both yeast and flies, the SC disassembles asymmetrically and persists associated with the centromere until late prophase (Newnham et al., 2010; Takeo et al., 2011; Gladstone et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In mouse spermatocytes, the SC is lost along the length of the chromosome but is retained at paired centromeres.
source: Similarly in mouse spermatocytes, the SC is lost along the length of the chromosome but is retained at paired centromeres (Qiao et al., 2012; Bisig et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Qiao et al., 2012; Bisig et al., 2012).

claim: The SC that persists at centromeres after the SC disassembles throughout other regions of the chromosomes promotes centromere bi-orientation thereby ensuring homologous chromosome segregation at meiosis I in yeast.
source: Studies in yeast show that the SC that persists at centromeres, after the SC disassembles throughout other regions of the chromosomes, promotes centromere bi-orientation thereby ensuring homologous chromosome segregation at meiosis I (Gladstone et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gladstone et al., 2009).

claim: In mouse spermatocytes, the SC that persists between the chiasmata after SC disassembly in the pachytene region is proposed to regulate local remodeling of homologous chromosome axes thereby promoting centromere and chiasmata functions.
source: In mouse spermatocytes, the SC that persists between the chiasmata, after SC disassembly in the pachytene region, is proposed to regulate local remodeling of homologous chromosome axes thereby promoting centromere and chiasmata functions, which are to ensure proper homolog segregation at meiosis I (Qiao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Qiao et al., 2012).

claim: The CO designation-triggered asymmetric disassembly of SC proteins and concomitant chromosome remodeling are set in place to ensure that the short arm of the bivalents can function in a manner orthologous to centromeres to promote bi-orientation of the homologs thereby ensuring accurate segregation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis I.
source: While chromosomes in C. elegans are holocentric, and therefore lack a localized centromere, we propose that the CO designation-triggered asymmetric disassembly of SC proteins, and concomitant chromosome remodeling, are set in place to ensure that the short arm of the bivalents can function in a manner orthologous to centromeres to promote bi-orientation of the homologs thereby ensuring accurate segregation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis I suggesting the existence of a conserved regulatory mechanism.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data and comparison with other organisms.

claim: Chromosome segregation at meiosis I in C. elegans occurs by outward pushing forces from microtubules assembling at the interface between the short arms of the separating homologs.
source: Further support for this stems from the demonstration that chromosome segregation at meiosis I in C. elegans occurs by outward pushing forces from microtubules assembling at the interface between the short arms of the separating homologs (Dumont et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Dumont et al., 2012).

claim: Both mammalian ECT2 and the ERK/MAP kinase are expressed in testis and ovaries.
source: Lastly, both mammalian ECT2 and the ERK/MAP kinase are expressed in testis and ovaries (Hirata et al., 2009; Fields and Justilien, 2010; Inselman and Handel, 2004; Nissan et al., 2013; Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some of the central region components of the mammalian SC, namely SYCE1, SYCE2 and TEX12, contain putative MAP kinase phosphorylation sites.
source: We have found that some of the central region components of the mammalian SC, namely SYCE1, SYCE2 and TEX12, contain putative MAP kinase phosphorylation sites predicted by GSP 2.0 ([Wong et al., 2007; Xue et al., 2008]; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The predicted ERK/MPK kinase phosphorylation sites in SYCE1 (S308) and TEX12 (S27) are conserved between mice and humans.
source: Moreover, the predicted ERK/MPK kinase phosphorylation sites in SYCE1 (S308) and TEX12 (S27) are conserved between mice and humans, and the S308 site in SYCE1 has been confirmed by mass spectrometry analysis as being phosphorylated in vivo in mice (Huttlin et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction and a citation to prior work (Huttlin et al., 2010).

claim: The S308 site in SYCE1 has been confirmed by mass spectrometry analysis as being phosphorylated in vivo in mice.
source: and the S308 site in SYCE1 has been confirmed by mass spectrometry analysis as being phosphorylated in vivo in mice (Huttlin et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Huttlin et al., 2010).

claim: A conserved mode of regulation for asymmetric disassembly of SC proteins is shared between worms and mammals.
source: raising the interesting possibility that we uncovered a conserved mode of regulation for asymmetric disassembly of SC proteins shared between worms and mammals.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the conservation of phosphorylation sites.
